concept.name: Bullish harami
concept.definition: A two-candlestick pattern appearing after a downtrend: an unusually large black body is followed by a small white body contained entirely within it. Technical analysts read it as a potential bullish reversal sign, interpreting the sudden contraction of range as selling pressure drying up; confirmation from subsequent candles is normally required.
concept.intuition: After a big down day, the market can only manage a tiny up day hidden inside the prior body, suggesting sellers have run out of ammunition and buyers are quietly testing the water.
concept.mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 is a long black body; candle 2 is a small white body with both open and close inside body 1's open-close range. The smaller the second body relative to the first, the more pronounced the conventional signal; a doji second candle makes it a (bullish) harami cross.
concept.failure_modes: As a mild two-candle formation it fails often in strong downtrends, where the small candle is merely a pause before new lows. CandleScanner-style statistics show only moderate predictive efficiency even with confirmation.
concept.misconceptions: It is not a strong standalone buy signal; practitioners treat it as a warning and typically require the market to break above the first candle's body. The second candle's shadows may protrude beyond body 1; only the body must be contained.
concept.example: In a downtrend, a stock prints a long black candle (40.00 to 37.00), then a small white candle opening at 37.50 and closing at 38.20. A close above 40.00 within the next sessions would confirm the bullish harami as a three inside up.
